title: Greek Columns Everywhere
objective: After this level you can spot Greek columns in modern buildings.
summary: The 19th-century Greek Revival copied Greek temples: Philadelphia’s Second Bank borrowed from the Parthenon, and the Lincoln Memorial echoes democracy’s birthplace.

cards.headline: Why does a bank in Philadelphia look like a Greek temple?
cards.body: Because in the 1800s, Europe and America fell hard for Greek temples, and started building them for money and memory.

cards.headline: The Greek Revival
cards.body: In the first half of the 19th century a style called the Greek Revival spread through Europe and the United States. Its architects based their designs on Greek temples of the 5th century BCE, and the Parthenon in Athens was a favorite model. For a few decades, looking ancient was the most fashionable thing a new building could do.

cards.headline: A temple for money
cards.body: The Second Bank of the United States, in Philadelphia, was built from 1819 to 1824. Its architect, William Strickland, took the Parthenon as his model, borrowing its columns and its plain pediments. An ancient temple became the template for a bank. Next time a bank greets you with a row of columns, you’re looking at a Greek temple’s descendant.

cards.headline: Democracy in stone
cards.body: The Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C., dedicated in 1922, has a reason as well as a look. Its architect, Henry Bacon, modeled it on the Parthenon because he felt a memorial to a man who defended democracy should echo democracy’s birthplace. Its 36 columns stand for the 36 states in the Union when Lincoln died. The shape is Greek; the count is American.

cards.headline: Greek columns: spotted
learned: The Greek Revival copied Greek temples
Philadelphia’s Second Bank borrowed from the Parthenon
The Lincoln Memorial echoes democracy’s birthplace

questions.prompt: What do the 36 columns of the Lincoln Memorial stand for?

options.label: The states in the Union when Lincoln died

questions.explanation: Each of the 36 columns stands for a state in the Union at the time of Lincoln’s death.

questions.prompt: Why does the Second Bank of the United States in Philadelphia look like a Greek temple?

options.label: It was built by Greek settlers
It was once an ancient temple
Its architect modeled it on the Parthenon
Banks were required by law to copy temples
options.rationale: It was a fashion, not a law.

questions.explanation: Strickland took the Parthenon as his model, part of the Greek Revival fashion for temple designs.

questions.prompt: Henry Bacon copied the Parthenon to echo democracy’s birthplace; from Level 28, which Athenian directed the rebuilding that produced it?

options.label: Solon
options.rationale: He is known for laws, not buildings.

options.label: Themistocles
options.rationale: He built a fleet, not the Parthenon.

options.label: Cleisthenes
options.rationale: He is known for reforms, not buildings.

questions.explanation: Pericles directed the Acropolis rebuilding that produced the Parthenon, the temple Bacon took as his model.
